implementation_notes: Scala's standard library ships the core value of the pattern: Deadline.now, the fromNow duration DSL and methods such as isOverdue, hasTimeLeft and timeLeft make an expiry a first-class, comparable value, measured with System.nanoTime so wall-clock steps cannot move it. Paired with a scheduler (Pekko/Akka scheduler.scheduleOnce, or a ScheduledExecutorService) it is enough to sweep a queue at the earliest deadline, and isOverdue is the check to run before any side effect. This monotonic guarantee is exactly why the deadline cannot be serialized: a distributed message must carry an absolute UTC timestamp, converted into a local Deadline at each hop, while the broker TTL (JMS/AMQP header) stays the enforcement point across processes.
pitfalls: Deadline is backed by System.nanoTime: it is meaningless across nodes and cannot be serialized, so a distributed message must carry an absolute UTC deadline and accept the clock skew it hides.
Deadline carries no way to be cancelled or reset - it is a value, not a timer - so a sweep still needs a scheduler and the sweep must be rescheduled from the remaining timeLeft, not polled in a loop.
timeLeft returns a FiniteDuration that can go negative only conceptually: methods assume it is non-negative, so check isOverdue before arithmetic on timeLeft.
